lesson.subject: anatomy
lesson.title: Vertebral column and regional vertebrae
lesson.summary: Typical cervical vertebrae have transverse foramina, thoracic vertebrae articulate with ribs, and lumbar vertebrae have large weight-bearing bodies.
lesson.section: 5. Vertebral Column Overview; 6. Typical and Regional Vertebrae

steps.title: Vertebral Column Overview
steps.body:
The vertebral column consists of cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal vertebrae. It supports the body, protects the spinal cord, transmits weight to the pelvis, and provides attachment for muscles and ligaments.

The usual count is 33: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and commonly 4 coccygeal vertebrae. Coccygeal number and transitional anatomy vary. Primary curvatures are thoracic and sacral kyphoses. Secondary curvatures are cervical and lumbar lordoses. The vertebral canal is formed by successive vertebral foramina.

steps.title: Typical and Regional Vertebrae
steps.body:
A typical vertebra has a body, vertebral arch, pedicles, laminae, vertebral foramen, processes, and notches. Regional differences let you identify the vertebra in practical exam.

Cervical vertebrae: small body, large triangular foramen, transverse foramina, often bifid spinous process. Thoracic vertebrae: heart-shaped body, round vertebral foramen, costal facets, long inferior spinous process. Lumbar vertebrae: large kidney-shaped body, triangular foramen, thick quadrangular spinous process. Sacrum: promontory, ala, sacral canal, sacral hiatus, auricular surface, sacral crests.

steps.title: How do vertebral facets and body size relate to regional mechanical demands?
steps.body: Lumbar bodies are large because they bear substantial load, while facet orientations influence permitted movement and resistance to rotation. Thoracic rib attachments add stability and alter regional mobility. Cervical vertebrae support head movement with smaller bodies and specialized upper joints. These are tendencies rather than one rule for every vertebra. Transitional levels often combine features. On an unknown bone, compare body proportions, foramina, costal facets and articular orientation before deciding the region from a single feature.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: Typical cervical vertebrae have transverse foramina, thoracic vertebrae articulate with ribs, and lumbar vertebrae have large weight-bearing bodies. C1 and C2 are specialized exceptions, and transitional vertebrae vary. The usual count is 33 vertebrae, including five sacral and commonly four coccygeal elements; coccygeal number varies. Primary thoracic and sacral curves persist from development, while cervical and lumbar lordoses emerge with head control and upright posture.
